one_liner: Rust/PyO3 asyncio event loop on io_uring, IOCP or kqueue; beats uvloop on TLS, bulk and TCP round-trips, not plaintext WebSockets.
what_it_does: A replacement for CPython's asyncio event loop, used like uvloop: `rsloop.run(main())` (a shortcut for `asyncio.run(main(), loop_factory=rsloop.new_event_loop)`), `rsloop.install()` to set the policy, or `rsloop.new_event_loop()`, and unlike uvloop it also runs on Windows. Your coroutines, callbacks and protocols still run as Python on the thread that calls `run_forever()`/`run_until_complete()`. Rust handles scheduling, timers, sockets, TLS, pipes, signals and subprocesses. Importing it monkeypatches `asyncio.set_event_loop` and, by default, `asyncio.open_connection`/`start_server` so they return a native Rust stream reader.
how_it_is_fast: Each loop runs a vendored single-threaded Rust runtime (vibeio): io_uring set up with SINGLE_ISSUER, COOP_TASKRUN and DEFER_TASKRUN on Linux (epoll via mio as fallback), IOCP on Windows, one-shot kqueue on macOS. On Unix a second runtime on the Python thread serves TCP protocol reads, so reads are not handed across threads. `call_soon` is a CPython FASTCALL descriptor that skips the argument tuple for zero or one argument, the ready queue drains in bounded batches, and before parking the loop busy-waits up to 50 us (reader workers 30 us) to catch ping-pong replies without a sleep/wake cycle. TLS is rustls on helper reader/writer threads instead of CPython's ssl module on the loop thread, which is the likely (undocumented) source of its TLS lead.
when_to_use: Asyncio services that terminate or originate TLS (aiohttp, websockets, Starlette/uvicorn): with 16 connections on the author's i9-9900K, TLS HTTP ran 72,496 vs 26,226 ops/s on uvloop, and websockets over TLS 26,781 vs 14,872, with lower p95.
Bulk streaming over TCP (large bodies, proxies, file relays): 2,009.9 vs 1,264.9 MiB/s in 64 KiB chunks, with p95 15.1 ms vs 25.2 ms.

Latency-bound request/response code built on `asyncio.open_connection`/`start_server` without TLS, where the native fast-stream reader applies: 5,000 sequential 1 KiB loopback round-trips took 83.3 ms vs 127.9 ms.
Windows or macOS deployments that want a compiled asyncio loop: uvloop does not build on Windows, while rsloop ships win_amd64/win_arm64 and macOS 13+ wheels.
Free-threaded CPython 3.14t with one loop per thread: the extension declares gil_used = false, so separate loops on separate threads run concurrently.
when_not_to_use: Code bound by callback or task scheduling: rsloop is only 1.10x/1.05x ahead of uvloop on 200,000 callbacks and 50,000 tasks (47.77 vs 52.67 ms, 88.29 vs 92.85 ms), and zuvloop beats it on both (36.77, 82.21 ms).

Plaintext WebSocket or HTTP keep-alive servers: uvloop wins on websockets (25,800 vs 24,667), aiohttp WebSocket and Starlette WebSocket, zuvloop leads HTTP keep-alive, and rsloop's raw WebSocket p95 is the worst of the three (4.45 vs 3.87 ms). The author's March 2026 Show HN post (early version) likewise found uvloop 10-20% faster on a synthetic FastAPI run, with rsloop ahead only on p99.

CPU-limited containers or busy hosts: the loop spins before parking and TLS I/O, add_reader/add_writer watches and parts of the write path use helper threads. The benchmark page warns that rsloop 'has more to lose when cores are contended'.

TLS setups that need full OpenSSL SSLContext semantics: the rustls backend rejects encrypted private keys and sets an empty server ALPN list (so no h2 negotiation through its TLS server). On servers it treats CERT_OPTIONAL as no client auth (only CERT_REQUIRED verifies client certs), and a server context must call load_cert_chain() after rsloop is imported.

Conservative or legacy environments: it is an Alpha-classified 0.1.x project, and patch releases have broken platforms. 0.1.34-0.1.45 refused kernels older than 6.1 and panicked where io_uring was unavailable (issue #75, fixed in 0.1.46), and Windows 10 broke until 0.1.49 (issue #76). Linux wheels are manylinux_2_39 only (glibc 2.39+, no musllinux), and subprocess preexec_fn is unsupported.

integration.form: module (CPython extension wheel built from a Rust crate with PyO3/maturin). The crate is also on crates.io for Rust extensions that return asyncio awaitables, but only up to 0.1.44, while docs/rust-extensions.md asks for 0.1.52.
integration.dependencies: No Python runtime dependencies. Rust side (compiled into the wheel): pyo3 0.29, rustls 0.23 + rustls-native-certs, io-uring 0.7 (Linux), mio 1, socket2, crossbeam, async-std, tokio (io-util only), windows-sys, plus a vendored copy of the vibeio runtime.
integration.min_toolchain: CPython 3.10-3.15 (3.14t free-threaded supported). Source builds need Rust 1.98.1 (pinned in rust-toolchain.toml, edition 2024) and maturin >= 1.9.4.
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64/aarch64 (wheels need glibc 2.39+). The README says Linux 6.1+, but master probes io_uring and falls back to mio/epoll, and that fallback path is not benchmarked. macOS 13+ x86-64/arm64 (kqueue). Windows 10+ x64/arm64 (IOCP; no arm64 wheel for cp310 or 3.14t). Other Unixes are refused at runtime.
integration.thread_safety: One loop per thread. A loop is single-threaded internally and asyncio objects are not thread-safe. call_soon_threadsafe() is the cross-thread entry point and keeps FIFO order. On 3.14t, separate loops on separate threads run in parallel.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same entry points as uvloop (install()/run()/new_event_loop()) and the standard AbstractEventLoop API, with integration scripts for FastAPI, Starlette, aiohttp, Sanic, Django ASGI, anyio, uvicorn, Granian and others. But importing it patches asyncio and ssl.SSLContext, TLS is rustls with narrower SSLContext support, datagram endpoints, sendfile and sock_recvfrom/sendto are Python-level shims over add_reader/sock_* calls, and preexec_fn is unsupported.

gotchas: Import side effects: `import rsloop` patches asyncio.set_event_loop, and asyncio.open_connection/start_server (non-TLS streams then get a native PyFastStreamReader rather than asyncio.StreamReader). It also wraps ssl.SSLContext.load_cert_chain, load_verify_locations, load_default_certs and set_default_verify_paths. Set RSLOOP_USE_FAST_STREAMS=0 to keep stdlib streams.
The headline TCP-roundtrip win depends on those patched fast streams. The benchmark's --no-rsloop-fast-streams flag gives the like-for-like run, but no result from it is published.

Tunables are read from the environment once: RSLOOP_WAKE_SPIN_US (default 50, max 1000, 0 disables spinning), RSLOOP_READER_SPIN_US (30), RSLOOP_MAX_WRITE_BUFFER_BYTES (64 MiB) and RSLOOP_MAX_PENDING_TLS_HANDSHAKES (256). Inbound reads pause at 1 MiB buffered per connection and resume below 256 KiB.

Runtime-initialisation failures have shown up as Rust panics ('failed to initialize loop-thread vibeio runtime') rather than Python exceptions (issues #75, #76). A loop that is never close()d leaks its runtime at thread exit. Client TLS handshakes are blocking and run in the default executor.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose rsloop over uvloop on Windows or when TLS, bulk transfer or stream round-trips dominate; stay on uvloop for plaintext WebSocket/HTTP servers, full OpenSSL SSLContext behaviour and a longer production record. Against uringcore, the other Rust asyncio loop, rsloop is the practical choice: it supports ssl= (uringcore raises NotImplementedError), ships wheels for three OSes and CPython 3.10-3.15, and is actively released.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's own harness (i9-9900K, Linux 7.0, CPython 3.14.7, release build with rustc 1.98.1 and fat LTO, uvloop 0.22.1, medians of 7 fresh-process runs), rsloop 0.1.52 did 5,000 sequential 1 KiB loopback round-trips in 83.3 ms vs 127.9 ms (1.53x), with rsloop on its native fast streams and uvloop on stdlib streams. A separate 16-connection sustained run of 0.1.49 gave 72,496 vs 26,226 ops/s on TLS HTTP (2.76x) and 2,010 vs 1,265 MiB/s on bulk transfer (1.59x), while uvloop won the plaintext WebSocket-library rows and the idle-wakeup latency gain was classed inconclusive.
status_note: Actively released (0.1.53 on PyPI 2026-09-15, 52 releases since 2026-03-21, 203 stars), almost entirely by one maintainer; Apache-2.0 with prebuilt wheels on PyPI and conda-forge, but still classified Alpha, and patch releases have carried breaking platform changes.
